'''Alanna Schepartz''' (born January 9, 1962) is an American professor and scientist. She is currently the T.Z. and Irmgard Chu Distinguished Chair in Chemistry at [[University of California, Berkeley]]. She was formerly the Sterling Professor of Chemistry at [[Yale University]].<ref name="autogenerated1">{{Cite web|title=Alanna Schepartz {{!}} College of Chemistry|url=https://chemistry.berkeley.edu/faculty/chem/schepartz|access-date=July 28, 2020|website=chemistry.berkeley.edu}}</ref>

==Early life and education==
Alanna Schepartz was born on January 9, 1962, in New York City and was raised in [[Rego Park, Queens]]. She graduated from [[Forest Hills High School (New York)|Forest Hills High School]] in 1978 at the age of 16. She then earned a B.S. degree in [[chemistry]] from the [[University at Albany, SUNY|State University of New York, Albany]] and a PhD degree in [[organic chemistry|Organic Chemistry]] from [[Columbia University]], where she worked under the supervision of [[Ronald Breslow]]. Following an N.I.H. postdoctoral fellowship with [[Peter Dervan]] at the [[California Institute of Technology]], she joined the faculty at [[Yale University]] in July 1988.<ref name="autogenerated2">{{cite web|url=http://www.schepartzlab.yale.edu/alannacv/AS.CV0709.pdf|title=Alanna Schepartz CV|access-date=June 3, 2019|archive-date=March 3, 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20160303184440/http://www.schepartzlab.yale.edu/alannacv/AS.CV0709.pdf|url-status=dead}}</ref><ref name="autogenerated1"/><ref>{{cite web|url=https://chem.yale.edu/people/alanna-schepartz|title=Faculty: Alanna Schepartz|publisher=Yale Department of Chemistry|access-date=June 3, 2019|archive-date=May 13, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190513151444/https://chem.yale.edu/people/alanna-schepartz|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Yale career==
Schepartz joined the faculty at Yale University in July 1988. She was promoted to associate professor in 1992, to Full Professor with tenure in 1995, and was named the Milton Harris, '29 PhD Professor of Chemistry in 2000. In 2001, she was named a professor in the Department of Molecular, Cellular, and Developmental Biology. From 2002 to 2007, she held a [[Howard Hughes Medical Institute]] Professorship. In 2017, she was named a Sterling Professor, Yale's highest faculty honor.  Schepartz is the first woman to be granted tenure in Yale's Department of Chemistry, and the first female Full Professor in any physical sciences department at Yale.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.yale.edu/opa/arc-ybc/v28.n30/story6.html|title=Alanna Schepartz named Harris Professor|publisher=Yale Bulletin and Calendar|date=April 28, 2000 |access-date=August 12, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20121021024924/http://www.yale.edu/opa/arc-ybc/v28.n30/story6.html |archive-date=October 21, 2012|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Field of study==
Schepartz works in the field known as [[chemical biology]]. Her laboratory is well known for the creative application of chemical principles to understand and control biological recognition and function. Her research has guided thinking in multiple areas of chemical biology, including the understanding of how specificity is achieved during protein-DNA and protein-protein recognition processes; how to design molecules ("miniature proteins") that function as inhibitors of protein-protein interactions; how these molecules can be engineered to reach the cell cytosol intact and with high efficiency; and the development of [[Beta-peptide|β-peptides]] as protein ligands and as building blocks of protein-like architectures.<ref name="autogenerated1"/> The development of β-peptide bundles was cited by ''[[Chemical and Engineering News]]'', a weekly news magazine of the chemical world, as one of 2007's “most important research advances”.<ref>{{cite web|url=http://opac.yale.edu/news/article.aspx?id=7154|title=Alanna Schepartz To Deliver First Chemical Biology Lecture|publisher=YaleNews |date=December 11, 2009|access-date=August 12, 2012|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110724185118/http://opac.yale.edu/news/article.aspx?id=7154|archive-date=July 24, 2011|url-status=dead}}</ref>

In 2017, Schepartz was appointed by Yale as Sterling Professor of Chemistry.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://news.yale.edu/2017/03/27/alanna-schepartz-appointed-sterling-professor-chemistry|title=Alanna Schepartz appointed Sterling Professor of Chemistry|publisher=Yale University|date=March 27, 2017|access-date=June 3, 2019}}</ref>

In 2019, she joined [[UC Berkeley College of Chemistry]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://chemistry.berkeley.edu/news/department-chemistry-welcomes-new-faculty|title=Department of Chemistry welcomes new faculty|date=May 10, 2019|access-date=June 3, 2019}}</ref>

==Schepartz Laboratory==
Schepartz is the Principal Investigator at the Schepartz Laboratory of Chemical Biology. According to the Schepartz Laboratory Website, the laboratory "develops chemical tools to study and manipulate protein–protein and protein–DNA interactions inside the cell. Our approach centers on the design of molecules that nature did not synthesize—miniature proteins, β-peptide foldamers, polyproline hairpins, and proto-fluorescent ligands—and the use of these molecules to answer biological questions that would otherwise be nearly impossible to address. Current topics include the use of miniature proteins to identify the functional role of discrete protein-protein interactions and rewire cellular circuits, the use of cell permeable molecules to image misfolded proteins or protein interactions in live cells, and the design of protein-like assemblies of β-peptides that are entirely devoid of α-amino acids."<ref>{{cite web|url=http://www.schepartzlab.yale.edu/research/index.html|title=Schepartz Laboratory of Chemical Biology|publisher=Yale.edu|date=|access-date=June 3, 2019|archive-date=June 4, 2019|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20190604145029/http://schepartzlab.yale.edu/research/index.html|url-status=dead}}</ref>

==Achievements==
In 1990, Schepartz was awarded a [[David and Lucile Packard Foundation]] Fellowship.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.packard.org/what-we-fund/science/packard-fellowships-for-science-and-engineering/fellowship-directory/schepartz-alanna/|title=Alanna Schepartz|publisher=David and Lucile Packard Foundation|access-date=June 3, 2019}}</ref> In 1991, Schepartz earned an Eli Lilly Biochemistry Fellowship, a Morse Faculty Fellowship from Yale, and a [[National Science Foundation]] [[Presidential Young Investigator Award]]. In 1993, she earned a [[The Camille and Henry Dreyfus Foundation|Camille and Henry Dreyfus]] Teacher-Scholar Award, and in 1994 received an [[Alfred P. Sloan Foundation|Alfred P. Sloan]] Research Fellowship. Schepartz received an A.C.S. Arthur C. Cope Scholar Award in 1995 and an A.C.S. [[Eli Lilly Award in Biological Chemistry]] in 1997. In 1999, she received the Dylan Hixon ’88 Award for Teaching Excellence in the Natural Sciences, and in 2002, she was awarded the [[Agnes Fay Morgan Research Award]]. In 2008, she was awarded the Frank H. Westheimer Prize Medal from Harvard University. In 2012, she was awarded the Ronald Breslow Award for Achievement in Biomimetic Chemistry.<ref>{{cite web|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/funding-and-awards/awards/national/bytopic/ronald-breslow-award-for-achievement-in-biomimetic-chemistry.html|title=Ronald Breslow Award for Achievement in Biomimetic Chemistry|access-date=June 3, 2019}}</ref> Throughout her career she has also been invited to be a distinguished guest speaker and lecturer.<ref name="autogenerated2"/> In 2014, she was elected to membership in the [[United States National Academy of Sciences|National Academy of Sciences]].<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.nasonline.org/directory-entry/alanna-schepartz-wjnabw/|title=Alanna Schepartz|publisher=National Academy of Sciences|date=April 1, 2014|access-date=June 3, 2019}}</ref>

Since 2005, she had served as an associate editor of the ''[[Journal of the American Chemical Society]]'', and in 2016 was appointed as [[editor-in-chief]] of ''[[Biochemistry (journal)|Biochemistry]]''.<ref>{{cite news|url=https://www.acs.org/content/acs/en/pressroom/newsreleases/2016/august/acs-names-preeminent-yale-professor-schepartz-as-new-editor-in-chief-of-biochemistry.html|title=American Chemical Society names preeminent Yale University professor Alanna Schepartz, Ph.D., as new editor-in-chief of Biochemistry|publisher=[[American Chemical Society]]|date=August 3, 2016|access-date=June 3, 2019}}</ref>
